## Overview of Plant Nutrient Uptake
<hr>

* **Review: Plants require many mineral nutrients for growth, development, and metabolism**
    + nutrients are absorbed primarily through roots from the soil solution

<br/>

* **Two main pathways for uptake:**
    + passive transport (diffusion, facilitated diffusion)
    + active transport (requires energy to move ions against gradient)

<br/>   

<div style="float: left; width: 43%;">

+ **Most nutrients enter roots as ions dissolved in water (e.g., NO₃⁻, K⁺)**
    + plants can't absorb solid particles directly
    + charged ions require transport proteins (in cells)

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:370px; LEFT:490px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:250px" SRC="images/transportreview.png">

## Root Hair Cells: Structure and Function
<hr>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:0px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/roothhair.jpg">

<div style="float: right; width: 45%;">

* **Root hair cells are extensions of epidermal cells in the root**
    + Increase surface area dramatically
    + No waxy cuticle, so water enters freely
    + High density of membrane transport proteins for selective nutrient uptake

<br/>

* **Thin cell walls and large central vacuole aid in rapid uptake of ions and water**
    + lots of mitochondria (?)
    
<br/>

* **Short-lived but continuously regenerated as roots grow through new soil zones**

</div>

## Active Uptake of Nutrients via Roots
<hr>
<br/>

* **Roots absorb scarce nutrients even when concentrations are higher inside the cell than in the soil**
    + passive diffusion would not work
    + ATP needed to transport across gradient

<br/>

* **Root cells use energy to pump out hydrogen ions (H⁺) into the soil**
    + creates a gradient that helps pull anions like nitrate and phosphate into the root

<br/>

* **Soil particles are negatively charged, holding cations (i.e. Ca^2+^)**
    + hydrogen ions also causes the cations to be swapped out into the soil water

## Root Structure & Nutrient Entry
<hr>

**Dissolved nutrients move between cells and through cell walls to reach xylem**

<br/>

**<span style="color:orange"> Apoplastic pathway: movement through cell walls and intercellular spaces</span>**

<br/>

**<span style="color:blue"> Symplastic pathway: movement from cell to cell through plasmodesmata (tiny bridges between cells)</span>**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:355px; LEFT:250px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/symapo2.png">

## Root Structure & Nutrient Entry
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 55%;">

**Casparian strips are located in the cell walls of the layer of cells that surround the vascular cylinder in plant roots (xylem + phloem)**

<br/>

**Forces selective uptake into symplast before xylem**

<br/>

**Symplast pathways uses plasmodesmata - small channels that are lined with plasma membrane (selectively permeable!)**

<br/>

**Allows regulation of molecule movement, prevents back flow, and prevents entry of pathogens into vascular system**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:0px; WIDTH:475px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/casparian.jpg">

## Mycorrhizal fungi: sharing with plants
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

* **~80-90% of plants have association with fungus**
    + fungi grown in/around plant roots
    + share resources
    + one of the most widespread mutualisms

<br/>

* **2 main types:**
    + Ecto- and Endo- mycorrhizae
    + diverse array of species for each

<br/>

* **Association now key for plants to thrive**
    + fungi more efficient @ nutrient uptake
    
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/mycorr.png">

## All Fungi share traits related to nutrition
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 58%;">

* **Use enzymes to break down compounds**
    + diverse enzymes for diverse food sources
    
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

* **Heterotrophs: absorb nutrients from environment**
    + decomposers: break down dead things
    + parasites: absorb from host
    + mutualist: absorb/share with host

 </div> 
 
<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:25px; WIDTH:450px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/fungienzymes.png">

## 
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:50px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:600px" SRC="images/am_em.jpg">

<div style="float: right; width: 55%;">

* **Branching hyphae used to exchange nutrients with plant hosts**

<br/>

* **Ectomycorrhizal fungi sheath cell walls**
    + *Hartig net* surrounds epidermal cells

<br/>

* **Endomycorrhizal fungi invade cell walls**
    + *Arbuscules*: highly branched hyphae inside cells
    + often called 'arbuscular' mycorrhizae

</div>

## Nutrient Exchange: Sharing is caring
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:10px; WIDTH:700px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/root_plant.jpg">

<div style="float: right; width: 35%;">

* **Inorganic nutrients imported to plant**
    + N, P and amino acids
    
<br/>

* **Carbon imported to fungus**
    + sugars from photosynthesis

<br/>

* **Possibly active & passive transport**

</div>

## Soil Life: Plant Roots, Fungi & *Microbes*
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 60%;">

* **Free-living microbial communities in soils breakdown organic matter**
    + plants cannot uptake organic compounds
    + fungi lost breakdown enzymes via evolution

<br/>

* **Microbial communities are carbon limited**
    + plants exude carbon (simple sugars) from root tips
    + exudates increases microbial activity

<br/>

* **Fungi are great at uptake and transport**
    + decomposers of *some* things
    + carbon limited
 
 </div>
 
<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:650px; WIDTH:300px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/exudate.jpg">

## Timing matters: Land plant evolution & fungi
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 60%;">

* **Fungal phyla associated with mycorrhizae diverged prior to the divergence of land plants**
    + Oldest fungal fossils appear ~900 mya
    + First terrestrial fungus ~ 460 mya
    
<br/>

* **What was the land like for first plants?**
* **What were early plants like?**

<br/>

* **Plant land colonization likely facilitated by interactions with symbiotic fungi**
    + fossil evidence shows similarity in timing
    + needs of both groups still relevant

 </div>
 
<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:655px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/liverword.jpg">

## Timing matters: Fossil forests and fungi
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 75%;">

* **Vascular plants evolved secondary growth (wood), with lots of lignin**
    + lignin is hard to break down

<br/>

* **~100 million years of trees sinking into swamps and not decaying**
    + carboniferous period = coal deposits

<br/>

* **Specialized phyla of fungi evolved as wood decay specialist**
    + ~295 mya (aka 'white rot' fungus)
    + lignin and cellulose

<br/>

* **What would the world look like today, without these evolutionary steps?**

 </div>
 
<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:5px; WIDTH:300px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/coalswamp.jpg">

## The current state of agriculture: Role of fungi
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 51%;">

* **Dramatic &uarr; in crop productivity last century**
    + development of pesticides, fertilizers
    + plant breeding and genetic technologies

<br/>

* **Now, crop yields have plateaued & fertilizer production unsustainable**
    + climate change
    + over population
    + nutrient depletion
    + energy prices

<br/>

* **High levels of fertilizer reduces fungal-root association**

<br/>

* **Big challenges to global food security**

 </div>
 
 <IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:525px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/fert.jpg">

## Role of mycorrhizae in agrosystems: Nutrients
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 60%;">

* **Crop species are breed to be hyper-productive**
    + fast growing with high yields

<br/>

* **Roots will rapidly deplete soil nutrients**
    + creates depletion zones around root

<br/>

* **Mycorrhizae extend the reach of roots**
    + widening the depletion zone

<br/>

* **Mycorrhizae access nutrients in forms plants cannot**
    + phosphorus from DNA or bound to minerals

 </div>
 
<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:30px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/depletion.png">

## Sustainable agriculure with mycorrhizae
<hr>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:700px; WIDTH:300px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/book.jpg">

* **Plant herbivory signals through fungal network between plants**
    + neighbors can turn on chemical defenses
    + fungi help induce these chemical defenses (VOC's)

<br/>

* **Nutrients benefits of symbiosis mean more flowers & nectar**
    + increases pollination

<br/>

* **Fungal hypae release polysaccrides that bind soil particles**
    + holds more water
    + stores more carbon
    + reduces  erosion & leaching
    + improves microbial biodiversity

## Are fungi always a good thing?
<hr>
<br/>

* **Fungal pathogens exist (non-mycorrhizal)**

<br/>

* **Not all crops have fungal symbioses**
    + broccoli, mustard,  spinach, beets
    + does this create competition?

<br/>    

* **Dependency on mycorrhizae varies greatly**
    +  wheat and corn varieties

<br/>

* **How far does 'sharing is caring' go?**
    + can the relationship become parasitic?
